description.preschool: A clade is one whole branch of the tree of life — a parent and all its babies, and their babies, with nobody left out. If you snap a branch off a tree, everything still attached to it is a clade.
description.elementary: Every living thing has ancestors, the way a family has grandparents and great-grandparents. A clade is one complete family on the giant tree of life: a single ancestor and all of its descendants — the whole branch and nothing but the branch. If you leave even one descendant out, it stops being a clade, because you have broken the branch.
description.secondary: A clade is a monophyletic group — one common ancestor together with every species descended from it. Clades are the natural units of evolutionary classification because they are real branches of the tree of life, defined by shared ancestry rather than by how similar things look. A grouping that looks tidy but leaves some descendants out is a "grade," not a clade: birds plus their dinosaur ancestors form a clade, but "reptiles" drawn so as to exclude birds does not.
description.university: A clade is a monophyletic taxon: an ancestor and the complete set of its descendants — the subtree produced by a single cut on the phylogeny. Clades are recovered, not stipulated — hypotheses inferred from shared derived characters (synapomorphies) or molecular signal — and they nest strictly, so any two clades are either disjoint or one wholly contains the other. Groupings that omit some descendants of their common ancestor are paraphyletic ("fish," "reptiles," cockroaches-excluding-termites); groupings stitched together from unrelated lineages by convergence are polyphyletic. Only monophyletic groups carry the inferential payload of common descent — predict a member's biology from the clade — which is why cladistics treats the clade, not the rank, as the meaningful unit. Clade membership is independent of Linnaean rank: a clade can be vast and supra-ordinal (Holometabola), tiny (a tribe), or correspond to no rank at all (Anthophila, the bees).

name: clade-taxonomy-relation
title: How do clades relate to taxonomy?

description.preschool: Scientists sort living things into nested boxes — small boxes inside bigger boxes — and name each box, like "genus" or "family." A clade is a real branch of the tree of life. Most of the time the boxes match the branches, but sometimes a branch does not fit neatly into a box.
description.elementary: Taxonomy is the naming-and-sorting system: each animal goes in a species, inside a genus, inside a family, inside an order — boxes inside boxes. Clades come from the actual family tree of life. Usually a family or genus is a clade, a real branch. But people drew many of the boxes long ago, by how creatures looked, before they knew the tree — so a few boxes accidentally leave out a relative. A termite looks nothing like a cockroach, so termites got their own box; but on the tree, termites are just one twig growing straight out of the cockroach branch.
description.secondary: Linnaean taxonomy is a ranked hierarchy of nested categories (order, family, genus, species), each a named container at a fixed level. Cladistics describes the same organisms by their branching ancestry. The two usually agree — most families and genera are clades — but they are different kinds of structure: ranks are stipulated and rank-bound; clades are inferred and rank-free. They part ways when a traditional rank, drawn on overall resemblance, turns out to be paraphyletic — excluding some descendants of its own ancestor. "Reptiles" (minus birds) and "cockroaches" (minus termites) are such ranks. Modern classification keeps redrawing ranks to match clades — Blattodea now formally includes termites — but the rank system can never perfectly mirror the tree, because the tree branches at far more points than there are ranks to name.
description.university: Taxonomy and phylogeny are two distinct mappings over the same organisms. Linnaean taxonomy imposes a small, fixed set of nested ranks — a stipulated containment hierarchy in which each taxon sits at exactly one rank; cladistics recovers the branching tree, a rank-free hierarchy of nested monophyletic groups. They coincide only where a rank's circumscription happens to be monophyletic, and three mismatches recur. First, clades fall between or across ranks — Anthophila is a clade with no rank, Holometabola is supra-ordinal — so the rank system cannot host every clade. Second, traditional ranks are frequently paraphyletic or polyphyletic, having been circumscribed phenetically before phylogenetics: Isoptera nested within Blattodea, the apoid wasps paraphyletic with respect to bees, the genus Drosophila paraphyletic with other genera nested inside it. Third, because ranks are mutually exclusive boxes while clades nest at arbitrarily many depths, no rank assignment can capture all the nesting — there are always more branch points than rank labels. Phylogenetic nomenclature (the PhyloCode) responds by naming clades directly and dropping ranks; rank-based codes (ICZN) respond by recircumscribing taxa toward monophyly while keeping ranks — which is why familiar names migrate (Reticulitermes' family; Philanthus moving from Crabronidae to Philanthidae) and why a genus split can threaten a famous binomial (Drosophila melanogaster). The working rule for a naturalist: read the rank as a name and a filing convenience, and the clade as the claim about ancestry — when they disagree, the clade carries the biology.

description.preschool: A rank is how big a sorting box is. Some boxes are huge and hold many kinds of animals; the smallest box holds just one kind. "Family" is a big box; "species" is the smallest box of all.
description.elementary: Scientists sort every living thing into boxes nested inside bigger boxes, and each box has a rank — a word for how big it is. From biggest to smallest the main ranks are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. A lion and a pet cat share the same family box, the cat family, but sit in different species boxes, because they are alike in many ways yet are still different kinds.
description.secondary: A taxonomic rank is a level in the Linnaean hierarchy — kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species — and each named group, or taxon, is placed at exactly one rank. Ranks are a filing scheme invented by people: they say how broadly a group is drawn, not how old it is or where it sits on the tree of life. Every organism is described by one taxon at each rank, nested one inside the next, so a species belongs to a genus, the genus to a family, and so on up to the kingdom.
description.university: A taxonomic rank is a fixed tier in the Linnaean hierarchy to which a taxon is assigned; the principal ranks (kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species) are supplemented by intercalated tiers (super-, sub-, infra-) when finer resolution is needed. Ranks are stipulated, not discovered — a family and a genus differ by convention rather than by any objective property of the lineages, and the rank assigned to a group can change as classifications are revised. Because the ranks are few and fixed while the tree of life branches at indefinitely many points, ranks cannot capture every level of nesting, which is the standing source of mismatch between rank-based classification and phylogeny. Rank also governs nomenclature: animal family-group names take standard endings keyed to rank (-idae for a family, -inae for a subfamily), anchored to the family's type genus under the ICZN.

name: binomial-nomenclature
title: Why do living things have two-part Latin names?

description.preschool: Every kind of animal and plant has a special two-word name that scientists everywhere share, like a first name and a last name. The honey bee's special name is Apis mellifera. Whatever language you speak, that name means the very same bee.
description.elementary: A common name like "ladybird" can mean different bugs in different countries, which gets confusing. So scientists give every species a two-part Latin name that is the same all over the world. The first part is the genus — the group of close relatives — and the second part picks out the one exact kind. The pet cat is Felis catus: Felis is the cat group, and catus is the house cat itself.
description.secondary: Binomial nomenclature, the system formalised by Linnaeus, gives every species a two-part Latin name: a capitalised genus name followed by a lower-case specific epithet, both written in italics, as in Apis mellifera. The genus places the species among its close relatives; the epithet distinguishes it within that genus. The name is universal and language-independent, and once it is validly published it is governed by priority — the earliest correct name wins. After first use the genus is usually abbreviated to its initial, as in A. mellifera.
description.university: Binomial nomenclature assigns each species a name composed of a genus name plus a specific epithet, the pair governed by a rank-based code (the ICZN for animals, the ICN for plants). The genus is the operative unit: the epithet has no standing alone and is meaningful only in combination, so the binomial encodes a hypothesis — that the species belongs in that genus. This couples naming to classification, and through it to phylogeny: when a genus is found to be paraphyletic and is split, species are recombined into new genera and their binomials change, while the type species fixes which daughter clade keeps the original genus name — the reason a famous binomial like Drosophila melanogaster can be put at risk by a genus split. Priority, typification, and homonymy rules arbitrate the resulting changes, so the binomial is at once a stable label and a falsifiable claim about a species' placement.

description.preschool: Taxonomy is sorting living things into groups and giving each group a name. It is like tidying a huge toy box: all the cars in one pile, all the blocks in another, and a label on every pile.
description.elementary: Taxonomy is the science of naming living things and sorting them into groups. Scientists look at how creatures are built and how they are related, then place each one in a nested set of groups — a species inside a genus, inside a family, inside an order — and give every group a name, so that people everywhere can talk about exactly the same kind of plant or animal.
description.secondary: Taxonomy is the science of describing, naming, and classifying organisms. It gives each species a place in a ranked hierarchy of groups, or taxa — species, genus, family, order, and on upward — and a unique scientific name governed by international rules. Classical taxonomy grouped organisms by shared features; modern taxonomy increasingly aligns those groups with evolutionary relationships, so that a named group ideally corresponds to a real branch of the tree of life.
description.university: Taxonomy is the theory and practice of delimiting, naming, and classifying organisms: circumscribing taxa, assigning them to ranks in the Linnaean hierarchy, and fixing their names under the relevant nomenclatural code (ICZN for animals, ICN for plants). It is distinct from but coupled to systematics and phylogenetics — taxonomy supplies the named, ranked containers, while phylogenetics supplies the branching hypotheses those containers are increasingly required to match. The central modern tension is that ranks are stipulated and finite while the tree branches without limit, so taxa are continually recircumscribed toward monophyly, and the discipline absorbs the resulting nomenclatural churn through priority, typification, and synonymy. A working taxonomy is therefore at once an information-retrieval system — a stable, communicable set of names — and a set of testable evolutionary hypotheses.
